bibliography.abstract: Human mobility has a profound impact on social structure and collective behavior, which allows individuals to reshape group structures in response to strategy information, acting as a double-edged sword for cooperative behavior. It can both disrupt existing cooperative communities and enable individuals to escape adverse environments and seek high-quality interaction partners. This paper surveys current research progress on the impact of mobility on cooperation within the framework of evolutionary game theory, focusing on specific mechanisms of passive escape, dynamic self-organization driven by active choice, and the core trade-off between migration costs and speed. Mobility, an individual's spatial response to local strategic information that turns location into strategic advantage, influences cooperative evolution by altering interactive information and environmental feedback, consequently affecting sustainable social well-being, such as collective benefits. Under specific conditions, this self-interested behavior at the individual level can foster macrosocial harmony, embodying the unity of individual rationality and collective cooperation. Furthermore, we also discusses inter-layer migration and information routing mechanisms in multilayer networks and extends the perspective to human-machine hybrid systems where mobile agents with information regulation capabilities can serve as information supernodes. Our paper aims to provide a unified framework for understanding mobility as a combined physical and informational driving force in the evolution of cooperation.
bibliography.title: Current frontiers in mobility and well-being

en.what: This paper reviews literature on the impact of mobility on human cooperation using evolutionary game theory models. It details how spatial responses to strategic information alter social well-being, analyzing specific dynamics including passive escape, self-organized migration based on active selection, trade-offs between migration cost and speed, and multilayer network routing.
en.why: It unifies physical movement and information processing into a single theoretical framework, explaining how individual spatial choices can lead to macro-level social cooperation and addressing emerging human-machine hybrid network structures.
